ST ATI'S. 312.8 CJTSDITS 1 he German journals give ihe following instance of summary justice (?) in Hungary. In the early pa>t of June last, a poor man and woman stole some aiiicles of food from a house in the village of Kiev ago Cceres. A little time after the thieves were discovered, and I he piincipal inhabitants of the place met, and without form or process, condemned them to death. They were taken out of the village to the side of a pit, dug for 'he purpose, and there knocked on the head like dogs. A medical man was then made to examine the bodies, and he having pronounced that life was totally extinct, the two bodies were thrown into the pit. which was filled up with stones The auihonties being made acquainted with this atrocity, which, however, is said not to be a solitary one in that country, ordered an inquest to be taken, but the result is not v et known.

The Imperial ukase relative to the dress of the Jews is staled, in accounts from the Russian frontiers, to have already produced some deplorable effects. In Bordiczew, a considerable commercial town in Volhvnia, where, as in many towns of Southern Russia, the Jews form the majority of the inhabitants, some young Jews appeared is the synagogue without long locks of hair; the Chassidim, a fanatical religious sect, prevailing chiefly in Russia and Poland, incensed at this violation of a sacred custom, fell furiously on the blasphemous. as they called them, thieateoing to tear them to pieces. All their representations that they had only obeyed the commands of the Emperor were unavailing. The Chassid exclaimed that the Emperor could not command them in a religious matter; that he might he the God of the Jawanisn (so the Jews call the Russians, or properly the Greeks), but he was not theirs; that they should rather suffer themselves to he flayed alive, than submit to such wicked orders. A dreadful tumult occurred, and two of the voting men are said to have expired under the ill treatment of the Chassidim. 15 of ihe Chassidim have already been sent to Siberia. What has grieved the unhappy fanatics worse than all the rest is. that before sottiMg out on theit jnurnev they had to change their national dress for that usually worn bv the exiles to Siberia, and that their heads were shaved, their long locks being of course the first sacrifice.

A considerable and at the same time singular robbery was committed on Thursday at an hotel in Paris. A Sicilian marquis arrived a short time ago, with his family, at Marseilles, with the intent of visiting Paris. At the Hotel des Ambassadeurs, in Marseilles, he made acquaintance with two of his fellow countrymen, who, as they said, were coming on a trip to Paris. On arriving in the capital these two travellers took u small apartment in the same house and on the same floor as the marquis. Their intimacy became closer, and on Thursday the whole party went together to visit Versailles. In the course of the morning the marquis lost sight of his two companions, nor has he since seen them again ; for, on returning to his hotel in Paris, he found that his rooms had been entered in his absence, and stripped of all his money and other valuables to the amount of 20.000f., and that both his new friends, who were no doubt the thieves, had decamped, leaving uo trace of the ditection they had taken.

Silence. þÿ A correspondent of the Courier Writing Irom Hartford, Conn, concludes an interesiing lettwr with the following anecdote and reflections : On Tuesday last 1 visited the Asylum for the Deaf and Donb, in company with lie v Mr. Gullaudet, the iirst instructer of the institution. It is worth a ride to Hartford to witness what may tie seen here. The cheerfulness ot the pupils, the facility with which they converse, the peifection to which the language has been brought, are all gratifying spectacles. 1 attended the morning devotions here, Which arc truly the most impressive that I ever witnessed, for 1 went to see rather than take part in the exercise. The prayer is offered by the Principal in the language of sigvs, to which the pupils seem very attentive. USEFUL HINTS. DIETRIC MAXIMS RGSttRCTlNO HRAt.TH. 1. The food should he eaten slow, so that it may be well masticated and mixed with the saliva. 2. Animal food is sooner digested in the stomach than vegetable, but is more slunuiating for the system. Flesh long salted t and dried hams, &.c , arc less easily digested than fresh meat. 3 Farinaceous and vegetable food is slower of digestion, but is less heating. 4. Solid food, or food of a certain fibrous or pulpy consistence, is more fitted for digestion in the stomach than soups, jellies, and all highly concentrated sauces. These latter are rendered more digestible by the addition of bread. 5. Fish are not so nourishing ns the flesh of land animals, but are of a higher nature þÿ The white fish are generally lighter, and less apt to disagree with the stomach than the red. 6. Boiling renders food more tender and digestible, although a considerable portion of the nutritive juices are lost. Animal food should not be over boiled. Vegetables should be boiled till perfectly tender. 7. Roasting dissipates less of the nutritive parts of the meat. Boasted meat is. therefore, more nourishing than boiled, though rather heavier. 5. The second or wheaten bread is more wholesome than the first or finest. Bread should not be eaten newly baked. 9. Condiments assist the digestion, and if taken in moderation, are safe and grateful additions to our food. 10. The mixing of two or three kinds of food at one meal, such as flesh and vegetables, &c., daily experience proves not to be tin-

salutary, if it does not lead to eating loo much 11. All repletion should be avoided; but the quantity of food to be taken at one meal depends entirely on constitution, age, habits, &c. 12. Health, and strength of muscle, &c, depend upon the completeness and perfection of the digestive powers, not so much upon the quality or quantity of the food taken. 13. Water is the simplest drink. Toast and water, water gruel, are useful diluents both in health and disease. 14. The stomach ought not to he over distended with fluids during or immediately after a full meal. 15. With weak stomachs, it is better to drink sparingly during or after meals. A dry solid meal requires more diluents than a fluid one. 16. Breakfast should consist principally of a fluid repast. 17. Dinner should constitute the principal me il, and should not be delayed till too late an hour. IS. 'Pea forms a grateful diluent three or four hours after dinner. 19. Supper, if taken at all, ought to be light, and should be taken an hour or two before going to bed. 20. Exercise should be used in the intervals between meals, but not immediately be fore or immediately alter meal. 21. Fatiguing exercise before a late dinner, when the stomach is empty, is sure to impair digestion.

The public will recollect that during the parliamentary session of 1844, much discussion was raised respecting the renewal of one of those many forms of legislative oppression from time to time imposed upon the people of this country. The object of this discussion was to save the people from the continued operation of the so-cailed act, þÿ for continued to be the terror of the public st rpreventing the administering and taking of unlawful oaths in Ireland." We had. then, recently been horrified by the exposure of a number of plots for entrapping the people within the meshes of this law, in all of which the police were proved to have complicity. þÿ Many of them had been concocied by that body, and, there was much reason to believe, not without the knowledge of individuals holding high offices in the force, and seated upon the bench of justice, and within the pre. cincts of the offices of the government. In truth this act ought to be denominated an " act lor facilitating the transportation of the þÿpeople. Under its provisions, it is sufficient to have found upon any individual papers, printed or written, containing signs or passwords of any supposed society, having illegal objects, in older to subject that person to transportation tor seven years. Some scoundrel. double dyed in villanv, is found to swear that a confederacy exists or has existed which has had, at some certain lime pass- þÿ words and signs w hich he enumerates. Then comes a policeman, in nine cases out of ten

the confederate of the informer, or conscious at least of the means by which the case has þÿ been got up," and lie proves that similar sinns and passwords have been got upon the prisoner. The prosecution is complete. þÿ The man can make no defence, and the law gives no discretion ; the unhappy victim must be expatriated to a penal settlement, not because a crime has been committed, but that wretches may riot in the price of blood ! We have no desire that crime should go unpunished þÿ we would not shield for a single hour those unwise combinations to which an untaught peasantry resort for the redress of untold oppression These combinations are doubly criminal þÿ first, because they are sustained by evil deeds; and next, because they retard the progress of those safe and real remedies which the friends of the people are anxious to secure for them But bad as these combinations are þÿ hideous hr are the crimes in which unhappily they at times eventuate, we would not have them repressed by the punishment of the innocent and above all, we would not let loose upon the people the bloodstained trallieer in concocted crime. We rejoice therefore to find that the discussions in the legislature last session have had their effect, and that this obnoxious þÿ this tyrannic provision, in support of which the Tories pleaded the precedent of the Whigs, is proposed to be repealed by a bill now before the legislature, which has for its object the continuation lor a period of two years the remaining provisions of the act to

which we have been referring We congratulate the justice of the country upon being relieved from such an iniquitous provision ami from the frightful villanies which were perpetuated by informers and their accomplices under cover of this provision. þÿ Dublin freeman's Journal.

Murdering in Jest. þÿ A very singular circumstance, involving a duel a< d death, took place at Cincinnati last Tuesday. An Englishman named Robert Bland kept a tavern in that city. On the afternoon of Tuesday (as we learn from the Commercial) Mr. Bland got to arguing with one Samuel Powell on the subject ol shooting at a mark, and each had been boasting of bis skill. From shooting at a mark the subject turned on duelling, when Bland went behind (tie bar in his tavern, and took up a pair of pistols, letting Powell take bis choice, signifying that they could determine the point by a dial of skill. As they both went out þÿ of the tavern door Mi. Bland said to Powell þÿ þÿ The pistols are loaded." They had agreed, it appears, to fire at a distance of twenty steps, but after taking their positions, in the manner of duellists, they each walked two or thtee paces, wheeled, and both lired ! The result of this was, that Mr. Bland was shot, the ball entering the right side, and then passing through the region of the rh(?st to the point of the shoulder blade, where it lodged. He lingered till about half piast eight o'clock next morning, when he died, leaving a wife and two children. Both parties in this tragedy were natives of England, and what led to it is a mystery. During the night following Mr. Bland stated that þÿ he had not intended to kill Powell, and was glad he did not - /Vet v York Paper. Hunt. ung þÿ Mr. Rrantley Berkeley being applied by the Society lor the Discourage- to

ment of Duelling to join it, declined, and in his reply remarks that þÿ at present the mere fact of whether a duel may, or may not be, remains entirely in the hands of the seconds ; the principal having once called in his adviser becomes a mere living pistol in the hand of another, to be fired at an antagonist, or into the air, or nut to be fired at all in case of an apology being sufficient. This, when men of approved worth are the seconds, should be amply sufficient for the guarding against all abuses ; I am, however, bound to admit, that when men incapable of conducting so nice an affair, from whatever cause their incapability arises, are placed in the situation of seconds, the duel then becomes a mere ungraceful scene of ruffianism, or it is turned into an event with which society is dissatisfied, and which disgraces rnther than exalts the characters of all þÿconcerned.

A Drunkard. þÿ An inquest was held at the Jolly Anglers, Kentish-town, on the body of George Carter, aged 41, late of Trafalgarplace, keniish-lown. The deceased had been originally a stonemason, and some time ago married a lady having a fortune of 500/. a year. As soon as he became possessed of the wealth he indulged in every excess, was seldom or never sober, and according to report, would drink thirty glasses of gin before breakfast. A disease of the lungs and liver, and ultimately delirium tremens , were the consequence. On last Sunday, while labouring under delirium, he attempted suicide, by inflicting several wounds with a razor on his throat and ahdoinen. He lingered until Tuesday, when death closed his career. ROMANCE IN REAL LIFE. We find the following interesting and instructive narrative in the columns of a provincial contemporary. The history is not an imaginary one, but is the simple record of facts. 'The railways have effected various wonders ; but no class of marvels is greater than that of the various new characters they have formed. Many of the attendants, superintendents, engineers, &c.., were brought up to a very different profession from that which they are now filling. 'The following instance affords a very remarkable illustration of this fact: þÿ !n one of the English counties on the Welsh borders, a youth found himself in possession of a large estate ; he was then at Cambridge pursuing his studies, and had achieved several academical victories, particularly in mathematics. His estate had been lelt to littn by bis father on the attainment of his majority, subject to the annuity of his mother, who w as left sole executrix, but she being one of those fond parents who give continual proofs that parental love is blind, allowed her son the fullest latitude in his expenditure, a large item of which was the cost and et cieleras ot a pack of fox-hounds. Cur young Cantab had scarcely "come of age" when his mother died ; and he had just united himself to n young and worthy girl. þÿ Shortly after his mother's decease lie discoved thai his estate was so encumbered, and the debts to which he was liable were so pressing, that a searching investigation into his affairs

became absolutely necessary ; this lask he undertook, and ascertained that he was not fai off the point of rum. With praiseworthy determination he resolved to sell off everything, and to stand before the world a free man. After he had disposed of his properly, and discharged all his liabilities, he found himself still master of a good house in London, and about 200/, a year. He had the good sense lo resolve to quit the neighbourhood, and retire into some distant part of the country, where, with his wile, he might enjoy the comforts and some of the clegarc.es of life, without participating in those expensive amusements which are connected with a high position in society. The gentleman who narrated this romance to the writer lost sight of his young friend on his removing from the country; some ten years afterwards he chanced to meet him in London, when he had from his own lips the romantic portion of our relation, " You know," said he, " that we left and came to London. It was our orfginal intention to reside in a distant part of the count iy, but as we had a house in town, we altered our minds and took up our residence within us walls. A very brief experience, however, proved to us that by remaining there we should be obliged to keep up an establishment far beyond our means, for although we were more llian 10 miles distant from shire. London is the spot to which the gentry of every county continually repair. We. iherefoie, recurred to our original determination of living in obscurity, lieinjj on 1 lie look out
for such retirement, one morning I saw in a duilv newspaper three advertisements of cottage residences ; one in Scotland, another in Westmoreland, and a third in North Wales,

. . - þÿ . þÿ 1 and my wife weighed the merits of each for some time, but they were so equal that we did but resolve and re solve. At length 1 cut out the three advertisements, put them into my hat, and mv hat upon mv head, and said to mv tvifet Now, Bessy, which evetfalls first, let that he our fate.' North Wales was on the table first þÿ to North Wales I hastened, saw and approved, and within a month we were snugly located in our cottage There for ten years I passed the happiest part ot my life. 1 spent niv time in fishing and shooting, « interspersed' with literary occupations, which my wife shared with the cares of rearing two hoys, with which we had been blessed since we had taken up our Welsh residence. Our lives were thus progressing, a ud we had begun to have serious thoughts tor the future in respect of our two sons, when one day a gentleman called and introduced himself by stating that he was an engineer from London, and was about to mark out the best line from t<» þÿ þÿ . and that he had been recommended to apply to me, as le understood that no one knew everv part of that country so well as 1 did, and that if I would oblige him with mv assistance he would have great pleasure in remunerating me. The payment I declined, hut readily tendered him any assistance in mv power, þÿ This accepted, arrangements for our labours were made, and in the course of a short time the line was rnaiked out and the arrival of the engineer-in chief Iroin London, was announced. The day alter his anival was

appointed for our going over the line ; I accompanied the t wo, and afterwards w e examined other parts of the country, but the chief engineer returned to our line, and, addressing im fir st visitant, said þÿ You have been most successful ; it is impossible to make any improvement bv t fie slightest deviation.' 1 am glad to hear it,' was the reply, but I did not maik out the line; you are indebted to that gentleman for it ' Indeed,' he observed ; but made no further allusion to it at that moment. We dined together, and in the evening the chief engineer took an opportunity when we were alone of saying to me, 'Mr. , 1 am so well pleased with your vvoik, thai I shall be happy to give you further employment ; mean while 1 must request that you will provide me with a plan and section of the line voii have marked out.' 'A what V 1 exclaimed þÿ 'a plan and section? Mvdenr sir, 1 never saw one m my life, except indeed it was the plan and section of my estate in shire, which unhappily 1 was obliged to sell.' ' Are you not,' was the inquiring rejoinder, an engineer?' 'Certainly not.' ' ' Then you must be one.'

" This obervation led to further inquiries and discussion, in which 1 found that my mathematical education at Cambridge was about to do me some service. At length Mr. þÿ then addressed rue þÿ ' 1 will send down two young men who well understand suivcying, mapping, &c. Do not let them know that you are not an engineer, but merely point them out the line. From your mathematical knowledge, and the observations which you have already been able to make, you will he able to prevent any suspicion arising, on their parts, of your not being pro. fessionallv an engineer. Observe carefully how tliev (hi everything, and then come up lo town with them to me; and I warrant that, with your aptitude, 1 will soon make vnu an engi ncer.'

8 T . 8 » ® a St A T S 3 ' At first I hesitated ; but seeing the prospeel which was opening before me, especially in respect of my sons, I accepted it. On returning home 1 could not avoid exclaiming to my wile þÿ Well, Bessy, fortune will favour us yet.' and to her surprise and gratification, 1 related the Conversation which had make so great an alieiation in our prospects. The two young men duly anived ; I carelully followed my instructions. By the time their work was completed, 1 felt assured that they hud done nothing but what I could accomplish wituout diliiculi v. 1 accompanied them to London and undertook an engineering task, winch 1 suc.c.esslully performed. By continued perseverance, I reached the position in which you find me. 1 am educating my boys in such a way that 1 trust they will occupy a prominent position in the wide engineering tielu Which is now being opened bj the railways in this country ; and, as lor myseil, believe ine, my present active, and, 1 trust, uselul life, forms a profitable contrast to that ol my lormer cavs.'

A Railway through tub Wilderness þÿ A lew years ago it was a fatiguing tour of many weeks to reach the Fails of Niagara from Albany. We are now carried along at the rate ol 16 miles an hour on a railway olten supported on piles, through swamps covered with aquatic, trees and shiubs, or thiough dense loiests, with occasional clearings, where orchards are planted by autieipalion among the slumps betoie the settlers have even had time lo lun up a log house þÿ The traveller views with surprise, in the midst ol so much unoccupied laud, one flourishing town alter another, such as Utieu, Syracuse, and Auburn. At Rochester he adiiines the streets of large bouses, inhabited by g(), 000 souls, where the Inst settler built his lug cabin in the wilderness only go years ago. At one point of our train stopped at a handsome new built station bouse, and looking out at one window, we saw a group oi Indians of the Oneida tribe, lately the owners of the broad lands around, but now humbly offering for sale a lew trinkets, such as baskets, ornamented with porcupine quills, moccasins of rwoose-deer skin, and boxes of birch bark. At the other window stood a welldressed waiter handing ices and confectionary. When we reflect that some single towns, of which the foundations were laid by persons still living, can already number u population equal to ail the aboriginal hunter tribes who possessed the forests for hundreds of miles around, we soon cease to repine at the extraordinary revolution, however, much we
may commiserate the unhappy fate of the disinherited race. þÿ Ly nil's Travels.

Memory and Revenue op Animals. þÿ " A striking instance in proof of the existence of these faculties in animals occurred some time since at the seat of a noble lord in Surrey. þÿ In the park are two large pieces of water, divided by a small isthmus, which widens considerably at one extremity, and at the time in question a pair of swans were the occupants. A doe and her fawn, belonging to a herd of deer in the park, coming down to one of the pieces ol water to diink, were set upon liy the swans, and the lawn, by their joint efforts, was got into deep water and orowned. After a considerable interval ol time, wheu the swans were one day in the wide part of the isthmus, ami thus separated from their clement, a rush wot made upon

- - þÿ ; them bv a number of the deer, which trod under foot and destroyed one of them. The bereaved doe must have had Some means of communicating her loss to the other deer, and of urging them to help her in her revenge; and the most remarkable part of the transaction is, that the deer must have had a kind of I consciousness of the fitness of the moment, when the swans were to a great extent defenceless, or at least deprived of their greatest advantage, and had no means of effecting their retreat to the water." þÿ Notebook of a Naturalist.

Fatal Poisonous Effects or Guano. þÿ The Medical Tunes record a case of death by poison, from the effects of guano. It appears that a farmer, living about three miles from Limerick, had been to town in the early part ot June, for some bags of guano. In his anxiety to get home early he assisted to fill the bags, and while doing so held one corner of each of them in his mduth. ''he guano was very dry, and as a natural consequence some of the particles of it went down his throat, and immediately alter lie felt a burning sensation internally. On returning home tie complained of the heat of liis throat ; his tongue became painfully swelled, and fiis lips and mouth excessively sore. He made light of it, however, thinking it would wear away. The Toad Sloughing its Skin. þÿ The following account of tins operation is from an eye witness of the process, and may possibly prove interesting. Mr. Johnson, gardener to R. Gardner, Esq., of Chaseley Hall Manchester, writes: þÿ þÿ 1 have bad two toads nearly seven years, one in the grapery, the other in ihe pinery. They lie under ihe floor (lags all day, anti come out on the approach of night to wander over t fie premises. 1 have evidence of iheir great consumption of beetles and woodlice, and I consider them invaluable keeping in down these mischievous vermin. On entering the grape house one morning in April last, 1 saw one of mv loads, squatting on the floor in the act of sloughing his skin. I was not in time to see the beginning of the operation, as the skin had already cracked opeu down the back. The creaiui

was in tfie act of seizing it with its mouth at one side of its neck, when 1 began to watch it. It had brought its hinder parts as near its head as possible, by rounding its back ; when it bad got firm hold with its mouth it began lighting with all its feet, evidently using no slight exeilion. Its lore feet were the liist to be got out, and I can only compare it to the getting a leg and loot out of a stocking, as everything came otF both from above and under t fie feet. The skin in the mean lime peeled oil the body and seemed to turn down and form a roll on each of its sides; and towards the belly, which was the last part to be freed. The greatest dilliculty seemed to be to get the hind legs clear ; whilst this was going on. and the creature apparently scraping its sides with all its four legs, the mouth was receiving the slough in the shape of a lengthened strip or roll. I could perceive no mumbling motion; the hold of the mouth seemed to assist very considerably in the process, as it kept pulling back with its head, but the skin was swallowed without any signs of mastication. For a time previous to this the toad had assumed an unusually dark colour. When the skin had left it, it was a mottled light ash-grey. Youth. þÿ How beautiful is that law of playfulness which governs the youth of all created animals ? How glorious that short lived era ol the blood when school hoys, and puppies, and kittens, enper and dance by a sort of instinct or necessity ! This irresistible gaiety is sot the result of superior health and strength, tt is the exulting spirit ol mere hie in the newly born ; an elementary joyousness which require no aid from without, which is not excited in them, hut is a part of them. The child in proof of its being, might say, in the spirit of the philosopher, I rejoice, therefure, 1 am. We, whom years and knowledge have invested with the prerogative of being serious, smile at the eestaeies of youthful levity will) a sympathy moderated by contempt. Poor, foolish creature, how happy it allows itsell to be ! Pleasant enough We exclaim ; hut, all ! it it knew what was to come! We shake our prophetic head when we see lambs frisking about Us and think of mutton. This triumphant sense of life has different degiees of duration, according to varieties in moral and constitutional temperament; it may give wav before its natural period to the shocks of accident ; sometimes it is prolonged almost to that term which We call our years of discretion, and sometimes it blurts out in brief transports through the gloom and cares of pet feet reason and melancholy maturity. Once in a wav, in a spring morning, perhaps, a gentleman of soberhabits feels himself, on the first taste of the air, very unaccountably disposed. If

he he in the country, he lulls incontinently to rolling in the grass, or takes to kicking his heels, or Iries a short run with a jump at the end ol it, with other caprices of motion which have nothing at all to do with getting on. or for which, very hkelv, he heartily despises himself. He is soon relieved. His habitual feelings and numberless little Circumstances of his daily experiences are at hand to quell his romping vivacity at a moment's notice. He feels a twinge of the rheumatism, or recollects a bad bargain, and we see no more ol his jumpings.

from Belt's Weekly Messenger, Jjondoit, August 25, 1845. RELIGIOUS EXCITEMENT IN G ERMANY-SERIO US RIOTS. Accounts from Germany gives deplorable account of the state of Saxony and other parts of Germany, in consequence of the religious excitement which prevails in that country, and which is every day increasing. On the Pith of August, a very serious riot broke out at Lcipsic. On that day Prince John of Saxony, the general in command of the Communal Guards, arrived at Leipstc to review the Guards. An immense crowd of the inhabitants assembled «n the occasion, who received the Prince on his arrival on the ground with shouts, hooting, and cries of þÿ Viva þÿRonge, þÿ Viva Robert Blum, and þÿ Down with the þÿJesuits. The review went off lor some lime quietly, but again the same shouts and cries were renewed, and the people were becoming very riotous. They sang the Luther's Cantique in full chorus, and, an appropriate song from Schiller's Robbers, Eine feste burg ist unsen Goth." The review, however, passed oil without any actual riot or outbreak, though the people were so exasperated and excited that they appeared ready for any mischief. In the evening a vast inass of the populace, and among them a great number of the students of the university, took possession of the square in front of the þÿ Hotel de Prusse," where the Prince had taken up his quarters. The Cantique was again sung, as well as the songs from Schiller and a good deal of excitement prevailed. At length some person threw a stone at the windows of the þÿPrince apartments, s and the

example was followed by thousands of others. The whole of the windows of the hotel were demolished in a few minutes. Fearing that the guard of honour attending the prince would not be sufficient to repel an attack if it were attempted, a regiment of infantry gartisoned in the town was called out at ten þÿo clock. Some attempts were made by the troops to disperse the crowds, but finding them ineffectual, orders were given for them to lire. So unexpected was the discharge that even those who were assisting the authorities to restore order were unable to get out of the wav. Upwards of 30 persons were killed and wounded, among whom were two gentlemen in the employment of the government. Nine persons were taken up dead on the spot, and five have since died. The Prince left Lcipsic at daybieak on the 1 3ih, but even at that hour a great number of the inhabitants were on foot, who hooted him till he was beyond the boundaries of the town. From the last accounts, it appears that the peace of the town was not again disturbed, but a great degree of excitement prevailed. It appears that the exasperation of the people against Prince John proceeded from the fact that he is one of the most open and declared opponents of the Protestant Church, and that as a member of the Council ot Stale he opposed the granting liberty to the now German Church to perform Divine Service according to the new forms. An affair at llalberstadt, where the Pastor Ronge was maltreated, led to the disturbance at Leipsic.

þÿ ®orr> þÿo HOW TO TREAT A WIFE It is not every husband who knows how to treat a wife 'The following admirable lesson on the subject should be carefully read and treasured in the memory of every husband, and of every one who contemplates assuming that relation, It rightly

improved, it may serve to nveit many of the troubles of fife þÿ change the clouds to sunshine and render its whole course snmmh and placid. We know not the origin of the article ; but that it is a good one þÿ an excellent one, we are quite sure. First, get a wife. Secondly, he putient. You may fiave great trials and perplexities in your business with the world; hut do not therefore carry to your home a clouded or contracted brow. Your wife may have had trials, which, though of less magnitude, may have been as hard to hear. Do not increase her difficulties. A kind conciliating word, a tender look, will do wonders in chasing from her brow nil clodds of gloom. You encounter your difficulties in the open air, fanned by heaven's cool breezes; but your wife is often shut in from these healthful influences, aud tier health fails, and tier spirits lose their elasticity. But oh 1 bear with her; she has trials and sorrows to which vou are a stranger, but which your tenderness cm deprive of all her anguish þÿ Notice kindly her little attentions and efforts to promote your comfort. Do not take them all as a matter of course, and pass them by. at the same time being very sure to observe any omission of what you may consider her duty to you. Do not treat her with indifference, if you would not sear and palsy her heart, which, watered by kindness, would, to the latest day of your existence, throb with sincere and constant affection. Sometimes yield your wishes to hers. þÿ She has preferences as strong as you, and

it may he just as trying to tier to yield her choice as to you. Do you find it hard to yield Sometimes i 'Think you not it is difficult for her to give up always! If you never yield to her wishes, there is danger that site will think you are selfish, and care onlv for yourself, and with such feelings she cannot love you as she might. Again, show yourself manly, so that your wife can look up to you, aud feel that you will act nobly, and that she can confide in your judgment.

This engine which is designed to act in the continuous and rapid discharge ol musket bullets as a column ot infantry, is the invention of Mr. Beningfield an engineer of considerable reputation in tus profession, mid who has for upwards ol seven years devoted his scientific knowledge to render perfect the instrument of warfare which his ingenuity has discoveied. The gun. a barrel, is placed above a small carriage which runs upon a pair of wheels, and may he drawn hy one horse at the rale of eight or ten miles an hour, weighing about ten hundred weight

or rather below that weight, and being light in appeatance, and having, when in position as the military phrase is, a third wheel, by which it traverses with ease and steadiness. It is supplied with halls by two chambers, one of which is fixed, the other being moveable, which is called the volley chamber, and may he made to contain any number of balls. It is estimated that a thousand balls can be discharged per minute. The volleys are discharged in quick succession, and while being reloaded the stationary chamber continues to supply the barrel, so that a constant discharge may be maintained for a week, or a month, or, at least, almost without intermission; the Uulltts tV»s of an inch in diameter, but a much larger bullet might be used if required. The range is said to be verv great þÿ probably hall a mile, or more. They pass through a three inch plank, and when discharged against an iron target they are dashed to pieces. Toe estimated cost of keeping this gun in action would be under 10/. for eighteen hours, and would require the service ot only lour men, though it would throw more bullets than would be fired by two regiments of soldiers in the same time The power, which the inventor will not divulge, is excited in a few minutes, and is kept under control without difficulty or danger to those by whom it is exoiled. This gnn was seen hy the Duke of Wellington a short time hack, when his Grace took so much interest in file invention, and expressed himse//

so satisfied with the results that he diiected the inventor to write to Sir Ge >rge Mori ay, the head of the Ordnance department of the army, and request his attendance at the experiments. Sir George, being unfortunately indisposed, deputed Sir Fredeiick French to attend Sir Frederick did attend, and in consequence of his representation, a deputation of the committee of the Royal Artillery department, Woolwich, were yesterday officially present in the piece of ground to the south of King street. Westminster, to examine the invention, witness the discharge of bullets &e , and report to the proper government quarter the result of the experiments, and their opinion. The deputation consisting of military officers, accompanied by scientific men, and by Col. Chambers the secretary, arrived on the ground at three o'clock, where they were received by Mr Beningfield, and the experiments immediately commenced. A vast number of volleys were discharged, the discharges were continuing without much intermission for upwards of an hour, and fully answering all the expectations ol those hy whom they were witnessed, and supporting the assertions of the inventor as to what his invention could effect. A plank, of three inches thick was at forty yards' distance from the gun, completely drilled through with the bullets : and the iron target at the same distance exhibited the great power of the engine, the balls being flattened, and resembling pieces of tinfoil It is understood that

the committee were satisfied of the efficacy of what they saw, and that their official report will be favourable. Her congratulations were so gentle at my escape from mortal danger, her words so earnest and soft toned, that 1 would gradually get better ; her tender hospitality so complete, and her light-morning dress so becoming, that she asked minutely more loveiy than before ; 1 inwardly blessed her, the cabman and inv start which gave me such delight. As the physician had given strict orders to keep my chamber quiet, and her attendance in mv chamber was evidently so cheering to my spirits I was fortunately freed from the visits of her lather, and 1 had the dear delight of seeing her alone. Several da\s passed in this reverie. I began to get beilter. How could 1 help myself? The young lady was still attentive, kind and soft-spoken and sympathetic. 1 thought 1 hud made an impression. At the end of the fifth day 1 was sure 1 had, and determined to speak, if occasion offered with other language than the grateful

glance of an invalid's eye. Being so much recruited, 1 expressed a wish to leave the house the next day, feeling that the claim on the hospitality of mv friends could not longer he extended to meet any emergency. This being known, the lather of my beloved eutercd the chamber, lie

apologized for not visiting me, and explained the peremptory nature of the physician's order to let no one enter my room unnecessarily, as long as there was the least show of danger. þÿ 1 murmured my gratitude to him, and expressed a fear that 1 could never repay the unremitting and invaluable attention of his daughter. 4 My wife, you mean.' Collision of Steamers þÿ Loss of one hundred and ihirly-five Lives. The Constantinople correspondent of the MtH'tring Chronicle furnishes the following particulars of a dreadful collision between two steamers in the Black Sea : þÿ "On the night of the 1 1 th July, in the Black Sea, about forty mile east ol the Bosphorus, a most dreadful catastrophe took place. Two Turkish steamers, the one coming from, and the other going to Trcbi- Sorid, came into sudden collision, and one of them went down with ilie greater part ol l.er crew and passengers The vessels wore the Scutari, commanded bv Air Dubbins, and the Medjehrai Tidjshret, commanded by Air. Lambert. The commander of each vessel was perfectly aware of the approach of the other full twenty minutes before the fearful event happened, and there was apparently no danger. But Captain Lambert, fancying lie had an Austrian vessel before him. to obey a rule of the Austrian service, put his helm a starboard, whilst the commander of the Scutari, following t fie rule of the English service, put his helm a port. T hus ihe former ran right under the hows of ihe latter, and the collision was inevitable. If boih commanders bad put their helms a port, no accident could have happened. Though it Was a moonlight mghi, there was a good deal of fog, so that the mistake was not discovered till it was impossible to avoid its terublc Consequence. The Medjehrai Tidjahret was struck between the fore rigging and the engine. The shock was tremendous. There

were a great number of passengers on hoard both the vessels, chiefly Turks and Italians, and an indescribable scene of dismay and confusion arose. As the Scutari is an old ship, and greatly out of repair, it was thought she must have suffered most, hut the contrary proved to he the case Whilst this was in doubt, however, her commander proposed thai the vessels should he lashed together, or that one should be taken in low bv the other, in order that if either of iheni should he found to tie unseaworthy, or in a slate of wreck, the sound vessel might t> able to rescue the ship's company and passengers of ihe other. This proposal was most unfortunately rcjeetcd. The vessels parted ; ihe Medjehrai Tidjahret dropped about a mile astern, and in the course of Jess than a quarter of an hour it was found that she was sinking rapidly. þÿ

The Scutari, which had got hut slight damage, then went to her help ; hut it was too late. þÿ Very few, comparatively, could be saved þÿ The boats of lite devoted vessel were so overcrowded by those who strove with frantic eagerness to make their escape, that they sunk at once, \hout 70. however, hv swimming. and dinging to spars, reached the Scutari, w.iere they clustered round the paddle boxes till thev were taken in t'aptain Lambert and an engineer were picked up by a boat of the Scutari. All the rest, 105 souls, perished. Their agony was a short one, but it was terrific As the Scutari approached the wreck she heeled over (die people on the de«k, like wild maniacs, were visible in the moonlight), and as the sea sucked Iter down þÿ as the vortex of waters she formed in sinking almost made the Scutari spin round with the motion, there rose a scream of utter horror þÿ a last sciw.un þÿ which those who heard will never forget Hut more impressive still was the passive resignation of the Turks; they sat motionless, muttering their praycis; neither hv cry nor gesture did they manliest any consternation. In impassive silence þÿ amid the shrieks of despair of Christians þÿ the fatalists met their frightful doom From the first sdnek to live sinking of the vessel not moie than half an hour elapsed. " The captains of the two vessels, vou will see bv their names, were English ; the engineers weie also English, Upon English navigation and en dicers, therefore, this terrible accident must tiling much discredit in

this part ol the world. Indeed, alter every account has been given, one knows hardlv how to explain it. Two ships on the broad sea, being perfectly aware of each other's vicinity, rati foul of each other, and nearly the whole of the crew and passengei s of otie of their pensti ! There has been a court of inquiry held upon the matter, hut the Turks who formed the court were utterly ignorant of nautical all airs, that nothing like a clear explanation was elicited. These Turkish steamers have now been for seven years commanded by Englishmen, and worked by English engineers, and out of 70,1 voyages they have only three times met with-accideiits. This fact may he some set off against the monstrous blundering which led to the leatful event 1 have just narrated."

Soon afier it came on to blow bard from the SE, and the vessel then ran into a current of air the very opposite to the one just expei icnced. We have now been favoured witli a letter from Ainab, on Mount Lehannon, mentioning that on the very same day, at about half an hour alter sunset (which brings it to very nearly the same time), the heavens presented a most extraordinary and beautiful, though awful, spectacle. A fiery meteor, composed of two luminous bodies, each presenting an appearance of being at least five limes larger than the moon, with streamers or appendages from each, joining the two, and looking precisely like two huge flags, blown out by a

gentle breeze, appeared in the west, remained visible for an hour, taking an easterly course, and gradually faded to the view. The appendages appeared to shine front the reflected light of the main bodies, which it was painful to look at lor any time. The moon bad risen about ball an hour before, and there was scarcely any wind at the time. We have also accounts from Erzeroom, in Asm M inor, describing a sudden lull on the gist of June of the thermometer (which usually ranges in the summer at between '40 to 44") to 0 ! and a further fall of Si more degrees during a heavy snow storm which

lasted three days, alter which the thermometer as suddenly rose to 41. The greatest consternation prevailed among the inhabitants, who thought the world was coming to an end ; and even accustomed as they ate to cold, it was only by kindling large fires that they could help from falling victims to its intensity. þÿ London Caper.

Longevity of the Canary. þÿ It is a disputed point among bird fanciers, how long a canary will live. Some say 14 years, others fix 16, as the extreme limit. 1 have kept one in my family between 13 and 14 years; his song, however, had ceased previous to his death at least a twelve month. 1 have now to record the remarkable fact of a cock canary being in good song, who is at the present moment in his 40th year ! 1 saw him a few days since, when calling on a friend at Shepherd's Hush He was well and hearty, in excellent plumage, and remarkably tame. His extreme age was by no means apparent ; on the contrary, he was quite sprightly, and uncommonly observant of what was passing. Ills present master and mistress have had him 18 years, and when they first took charge of him he was more than 40 months old. I need not add that he is, in every sense, " one of the family." How much longer he may remain so 1 cannot say, hut lie looks so well that an insuiance might, 1 think, l>e effected on iiis life for at least five years to come. þÿ IK. Kidd (in Gardener's Chronicle).

Three ol the peas were presented by T.J lYttigrew, Esq, to Mr. W, Grimston, of ibe Herbary, Highgate; but it was not fill last year that Mr Grimston resolved to ascertain whether they still retained the powers of vegetation ; and in June he planted them in a compost, resembling as nearly as possible the alluvial soil of the Nile, and placed them in a forcing frame, and in a short time he was agreeably surprised to find them sprouting, and they ultimately produced 19 pods, from which 55 peas were preserved. From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London, September 1, 1845. SPAIN. Insurrection in Madrid aoainst the Income and Property Tax. þÿ It appears that the Spanish minister has not been so successful as Sir 11 Fed. There exists at the present time a general movement in Spain against the Income and Property Tax, which in imitation of his brother Premier in England, the Spanish minister had imposed upon the Spanish people The people, upon their patt, have borrowed also a mode of resistance from an example recommended by Mr. O'Connell in Ireland þÿ that of passive resistance; by shutting up their shops, and thus, as the proclamation states it, þÿ hoping to create a rebellion by depriving the people of the articles necessary for their subsistence and þÿwants. In order to defeat this object the government has not been wanting in due vigour upon its own part. The Governor published a proclamation commanding all shops to be opened within four hours after the notice given in the proclamation ; all persons to he deemed rebels, and to be arrested and brought or. the instant before a special commission, who should refuse or delay obedience. In order the better to secure compliance with this order, tlte protecting commissaries of public safety, and the district commissaries, after the expiration of the specified four hours, were ordered to proceed street by street, and to make out and to bring up to the governor a list of the shops closed. The special commission before whom the persons are brought up and tried seems to he verv much like a drum head court martial, as

the accused are found guilty as a matter of course, and sent olf immediately to he shot. Hut. with the usual audacity of these despotic administrations, it is at the same time announced to the public that the Cabinet will not consent to supersede the ordinary tribunals, it iid to proceed by court martial in offences cognisable by the civil and criminal courts. Though we should very seriously lament that the present Spanish government should he overthrown bv this popular commotion, we feel it rlillicult to excuse the Spanish minister for the needles peril into which he has brought the government, and for the imposition of a tax so justly odious to a free people as the income and property tax. It was carried in England during the first days of the popularity of Sir It. Feel, and he has contri- of ved to get it continued hv the application a system peculiar to þÿhimself that of buy ng off all the stronger opposing interests. Hot in Spain the tax is wholly new, and as tlx logicians sav. of first impression; the people have not known it long enough to become familiar with its deformities, and, therefore, like vice itself, to he hated it needs only to he seen In former days, the most especial wonder of foreigners was. that such a free countrv as England could tolerate Hogging in its army and navy The foreign wonder of the present day is that we have suflered the minister to continue the Income tax. Hut this is one of those things which w ill doubtless be remembered at the next general election.

In one of these groups was a young ami beautiful woman of about 18 yea is of age, wlio appeared sorrowful and dejected, and whose neat and unpretending dress little resembled the bridal costumes of some of the gayer voiaries of Hymen. On the other side of the hall sat two young persons who appeared to wait with great impatience the arrival of a third person, whose presence was altogether indispensable. It was, in fact, no other than the bridegroom for whom they were so anxiously looking out. At length a carriage arrived, and a young man stepped out. Docs and Panoehs. þÿ VVe copy the following communication from the Liverpool Mercuiy, to the editors of which it ha been addressed by A Friend of the late Egerton þÿSmith þÿ : As a friend of (he canine race I beg you will favour me by the insertion of the following bit of advice to the owners of dogs. If the magistrates order you to muzzle your dogs, muzzle them by all means, but do it humanely, that is, by a light wire muzzle or strap ; but in either case allow the dog to put out his tongue, and take care to let him have water when tie wants it. Canine madness has nothing to do with the weather, although such an opinio, is popular. Pogs don't go mad in Turkey, Barbary, Egypt, or Sicilv, where they abound, and where the heal in summer far exceeds that of our hottest days: but they can drink at all limes at the overflows of the fountains in the streets. We have no such useful, to say nothing of ornamental, works, to which man and beast can have access, and it is the more incumbent on owners of dogs here to attend to their wants. Dogs may probably be driven mad bv thirst unallaved The few eases of hydrophohia Liverpool have occurred in Ihe in winter or m the months next to (fiat season, which fact ought to tie borne in mind by our medical men, who might so use their influence with our magistiates as to induce them to do away with the old dog day humbug þÿ Before I conclude, allow me to beg all birdfanciers to bang the cages in the shade, and not or, a hot wall exposed to the rays of the
aun. þÿ B.il' t Weekly Messenger.

From þÿBell s Weekly Ahttenger, Loudon, September 1, 1845. DISTURBANCES AT MADRID. Disturbances of a serious nature have broken out in Madrid, in consequence of the new system of taxation adopted by M. Mon. the Minister of Finance. þÿ his I scheme, according to which the taxes are to be uniformly assessed and collected throughout Spain, has given great displeasure to several provinces, such as Catalonia, Aragon, and Valencia which will have to pay much highei taxes than what they have hitherto been accustomed to. Navarre and the Basque provinces have manifested still more hostility to M. þÿMon s system In the capital itself the scheme has been viewed with very great aversion. A meeting of the merchants, manufacturers, and tradesmen of Madrid was held, and a petition to the Minister of Finance was agreed upon, praying that be would postpone the execution of his measure, and declaring, at the same time, that a great many warehouses and shops most be closed if he persevered in it. M. Mon declared that he would not abandon his plan. Considerable agitation was soon observable among the commercial classes. On the 17th, a large number of tradesmen assembled, in order to concert together a demonstration against the new system ol taxation, by means of a genera! closing of their shops. On the following day a great many shops were closed, but the demonstration was not general in consequence of it being agreed that another dav should be allowed to the minister. No change, however, taking place in his determination, the l!Jth saw nearly the whole ol the shops closed,

and the discharged workmen parading the streets. During the day a collision occurred between the troops and the people; hut the latter were dispersed, with the loss of a few lives. A proclamation was issued forbidding, under-severe penalties, the closing of the shops. This proclamation was, however, unheeded ; and on the morning of the 20th the Political Chief, accompanied by the commissaries of police, and about 100 mounted men of the civic guard, commenced making his rounds to summon the shopkeepers forward to open their establishments. They knocked at every door as they passed, and receiving no reply from within, the Commissary iw- Chief made a list of those who refused to obey tile summons, and then passed on his way to others Operations were commenced in the Calle de Oarretas. On arriving in the Callc de 'Toledo, ami the Barrios Vajos, the shops were also found closed, and on being summoned to open the masters daringly replied that they would do no such thing. Provoked, no doubt, by the bold manner in which the negative was given, the aimed police were ordered to force open the doors with their muskets. They did so; and some employed axes to effect the operation when the muskets had failed. In the Plaza del Progreso, ot® man, a Gallego, held a dialogue from his balcony with the Political Ohief. Tranquilly smoking his cign , he told that functionary that the government ruled in Spain, but that his house was his own little kingdom, and that there he should command with absolute authority ; that, besides, he had

iosl all 'aste for business of a low kind ; he should no longer distribute candles, gat ban- -)», and cabbage to his customers, of whom he had taken a long farewell, ns he was shout to set out ou bis navels to Home ; and wish-

rig the Political Chief, his commissaries. Civic Guard, and two pickets of cavalry, a verv good mrning, he retired from the balcony, and closed the shutters. Four of the police mounted the balcony, entered the house, and opened the door from the inside They were scarcely gone a few yards from the door, when it was again closed. The police returned and took the orator prisoner. After having made his rounds, the Political Chief made a second visit to tire places he had left; and to his vexation found all the doors again shut as before. They were again forcetl open, and pickets of infantry were placed at short intervals to watch and prevent their being closed a second time. The operations near the Puerta de Toledo, and the neighbouring streets, which ate the St. þÿGile s and Whitechapel of Madrid caused a considerable crowd to be collected. The troops in clearing the people Irorn lire pathways wounded some persons; and one very respectably dressed man, who was looking on from curiosity, was killed by a soldier, who pierced him wiih his bay met. An ingenious mode was adopted by some of baffling the authorities. On many doors were primed notices to lei, and an intimation iri writing that the owners had retired from business altogether. On some it was announced that the property was to he sold forthwith, as well as the good will of the house; and a bookseller in the Calle del Carmen had a notice to the eliect, that as he found himself unable to pay the exorbitant contributions imposed by the government, he

was ready to s.-.ll off his stock and retire from business. One witty Andalusian, in the Plaza Mayor, gravely informed the Political Chief that lie was just named private tutor to the children of Madame Munoz, and that he had given up selling leather gaiters and montern caps. Another sttnll and tobacco dealer it is said, affirmed that he was nearly related to the mother in law of the Queen- Mother, and hoped they would have a due regard to the alliance he had with the Itnvnl Family. þÿ1 he provision shops, a few cafes, and the þÿapothecaries shops continued open. Our latest accounts, which come down to the 22d, state that Madrid was tranquil, and that, notwithstanding the arrest of a great number of tradesmen, many of the slurps were only half opened.

A Kingly Mind þÿ The following anecdote, which we extract from a work translated from the German, may be new to some of our readers. To all, but especially to the young and gentle, it will he very acceptable: þÿ þÿ The Empress of Kussia trad presented to her revered father (Frederick William 111. of Prussia) an Asiatic plant, of brilliant colour ami agreeable odour þÿ a flower until then unknown in Germany. It was entrusted to the at tistical court gardener, Fintlemann, to be placed in the Palmhouse on the Peacock Island, amongst other exotics. The King took great pleasure in this scarce plant, and named it after his beloved daughter, Charlotte. Whenever he visited the island, his first enquiry was. þÿ How thrives my þÿCharlotte? which naturally caused the gardener to pay a more than usual attention to the favourite. The public were permitted to visit the island two days in every week during summer, and thousands flocked to the spot to inspect the choice collection of exotics. Who can describe the feelings of the careful gardener when he discovered one day that some one had plucked and borne off the favounte flower. He rushed through the crowd of visitors, eyeing each individual in hope of discovering the stolen jewel After a search, he fixed him-elf at lie landing place by which visitors must return. He had not waited long when a young and well dressed man came on, þÿw ith the identical flower displayed in the buttonhole of his coat Seized and questioned as to the robbery, he excused

himself on the score of ignorance, and sorely regretted the thoughtless deed. The offended gardener dragged the amazed stripling to his dwelling, that in the presence of three witnesses a protocol might he taken of the affair, and laid before the King, as exculpatory of himself. His Majesty, ere long, came to the island, and as usual asked þÿ How thrives my Charlotte þÿT The court gardener, with tears in his eyes, related some of the particulars. Though evident displeasure marked the Kino's countenance, he calmly remarked, It was unkind to deprive me of that small þÿjoy. þÿ 1 þÿThere ll be no end to such conduct,' said the angry gardener, þÿ if your Majesty does not forbid the public visiting the island þÿ How can the public help,' said the King þÿ that amongst thousands, an ill behaved one should abuse the permitted liberty ? The island was not placed there for me alone ; you know 1 can only find time to visit it occasionally; wherefore, then, these beautiful and quickly fading flowers, þÿ am I alone to enjoy the sight of them þÿ? The gardener begged that the committed robbery might be examined into, and the offender punished. As he motioned to hand in the protocol, and was about to mention the þÿculprit name, s the King abruptly stopped him, saying, No, no, 1 de þÿ sire not to know Jhts name; þÿ 1 have an unlucky memory ; þÿ hereafter the man may have occasion to ask some favour, and his name causing ine to recollect the unpleasant circumstance, tend to his disadvantage. From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London August 18, 1843. Hurricane in Norfolk. þÿ On Saturday, we were visited by one of the most extraordinary storms that have swept over us for manv years. A gentleman of our acquaintance first saw it, while between Pukefield sod Lowestoft, coming inside the Newcombe Sand. It continued to sweep along the coast, till it came to Gorleston Pier, where it crossed just over the residence of Captain Smythe, R. N but with no great violence. It proceeded thence, at a terrific rate, along the east bank of the river, across the gas works, where it took off part of the roof from the retort house, as well as from the puiifying and the tar-houses, which are much lower buddings. As it swept over the north gasholder, the men employed on the works wa re greatly alarmed lest the large body of gas should escape, and produce an explosion They described the holder, which is substantially fitted inside, as being completed collapsed. Several boats in Mr. þÿBeeching syard, adjoining the gas works, were blown over, awd many were lifted out of the water. The crane at the Trinity whaif, which was fastened down to a 14 cwt. iron sinker, laying on the ground, was blown round and stopped onlv bv falling against ihe house. Three or four men on the wharf were obliged to throw themselves flit on the ground, and seise the mooring rings, to prevent being blown a wav. The south door of the Trinity warehouse being open, the wind entered, and lilted part of the roof, o that the puilms we>e separated seven inches from the principals, dama-

ging the walls, although the roof was tied on verv seeurelv, which alone prevented its being carried away altogether. A boat, sixteen feet long, was carried a distance of fifteen vards; and several trees we e grvatly damaged, while others were not even touahed, although at a few yards distant therefrom. The river was lashed to foam, and threw up Its spray twenty yards high. The Resolution, London trader, was thrown on her side, so that her keel was clean out of the water, and but that she was well moored she would probably have gone over, and sunk. Yet, on the other side of the water, it was quite calm. On the quay, many of the trees wore damaged, an<l several swallows and sparrows were dashed to the ground, and either killed or stunned so as to be easily taken þÿ Near Shelly and þÿCo s warehouse, a quantity of coalheaver's shovels were caught up, and

In Charlotte-street, a quantity of paper-hangings, fi.ii., exposed for sale, were blow awn v. The current of air which seemed to sweep every thing in its track, appeared to be unusually narrow. It beat its course through the market down to the north river and across to the sea, dismasting the brig Enchantress, and a sloop lying in the wold During the hurricane, a young female, named Susannah Muttit, apprentice to Mrs. Carbarn, while returning to work after dinner, was caught bv the wind, and thrown violently into a pool of water 5 a policeman, who witnessed the accident, assisted hoi up. COM MERC1AL INTERCOURSE WITH CENTRAL AFRICA. We copy from Le Const itutinnnel the following interesting article on the subject of the internal commerce ol Africa : þÿ þÿ The fact is now placed beyond a doubt, that a very considerable commercial movement formerly existed between the Barbary regencies, Morocco, and the interior of the African continent. The want of security may. perhaps, have retarded it for some years, but the tendency, the necessities, and the habits of the people still remain, and it will tie possible, by well organised efforts, to restore to this commerce all its importance. The routes bv which the goods and mer chandise disembarked at liona, Algiers, or Oran, arc conveyed are at present perfectly well known. Upon these routes are observed towns which serve as magazines or storehouses for the caravans, or ns entrepots for the commodities; such seem to advance abreast towards the Desert. Thus Constantine, .Vledeab, Mascara, and Tlemcen form, on departing from the sea shore, the first line of maikeis for the produce of Europe, T'bessa, Riscara, Hougaada, l.agltouat, and Ntiiten, constitute the second line ; and on the third, we find the Oued-Souf, Toggurt, Ouerguela, and Meltili. Farther on, but

S "J\ V 3i t> 'I z At'13. still presenting themselves in a parallel line, aie El-Sedames, El-Colea, and El- A rib. The merchandise which, from these three last points, is sent forward towards the south, meets on its route with a most important maiket, dial divines the crossing of the Desert and forms die great oasis ol Touar. From this station the caravans, which arc there assembled In concentration, take different routes, in older to proceed to the various parts of the Soudan. þÿ Our readers are aware that all commerce in tiiat country is carried on hv means of caravans. Exposed to the attacks and the robberies ol the inhabitants of the Desert, the merchants are compelled to purchase the protection of the chiefs of these pirates of the Sahara. Amongst these tribes, the greatest and most numerous is, without doubt, that of the Tourareg. They are excellent horsemen, and from time immemorial they have enjoyed the ptivilege of providing the escorts tor die protection of the passage of the caravans. þÿ The Touaregs arc a Barbary race ; they profess the .Mussulman religion according to the Alalekite rites ; it is said that they have a pale complexion, and that they wear pantaloons which strongly rwsemble in their closely filling lorrn the pantaloons of the Europeans. Their women have blue eyes, and some of them are surprisingly pale. They (the women) smoke a gieat deal, and are considered very passionate; they cultivate poetry with maiked taste. It is related by Arabs who have made several journeys with the Tona-

regs, that these nomads are in the habit, when they cross the Desert, of placing inscriptions upon all the stones with which they meet. þÿ These inscriptions, which are most frequently in verse, set forth the lofty deeds of the writer, or otherwise, challenges to an enemy, or the praise ol a favourite flame. It is not uncommon to find verses addressed to an unknown beauty, in which the poet hopes to soften the heart of the first beautiful gill who shall chance to read them. The woman who desires to reciprocate the love of the poet writes under the first inscription a reply, wherein she betrays her name, and makes herself known. This amorous correspondence is very frequent. þÿ But what is still more curious, and worthy of riveting the attention of all our archaeologists and philologists, is the fact that these inscriptions are written in characters which do not resemble in the slightest degree the Arabic characters, and which the natives look upon ns the written alphabet of the Targuia, or Barbary tongue. The most credible conjectures give reason to believe that these characters are borrowed from the Phoenician writings. þÿ At Ouerguela there are Artesian wells hollowed out ol the stone, and the piercing of which is ascribed bv the tradition of the country to Alexander the Great. From Tuggnrt to Timbucroo, the caravans arc 87 days on the road, including 29 incampinents ; but eight days are devoted to repose at dif ferent parts of this long march. It will be easy to render still more complele the infor-

mation that has been already collected respecting the Sahara, and the manners of its inhabitants, l>v sending native explorers, already initiated in European civilization, who will he able to penetrate without danger into the very centre of Africa. þÿ

þÿI karl Divers. þÿ The Yaquis are expert divers for pearls in the Gulf of California. þÿ F'.very season, eight or ten small vessels, from filteen to forty tons, manned by about two hundred diveis. repair to different parts ol the Gulf The pearls, as is well known, are contained in the shells of oysters, and of some smaller fish ; and these do not lie on sand banks at a moderate depth, but are often fastened to roeks, or in the clefts of rocks, from nine to eighteen feet below the surface. There are many, no doubt, much deeper ; but as the diving bell cannot be employed the operation, they are inaccessible in to the divers. To descend eighteen, or fifteen, or even twelve feet in the water requires no slight muscular strength; nor is it easy to remain underneath time enough to snatch the shells from the rocks, when they happen (as is often the case) to cling tenaciously. Sometimes the hands and feet of the divers are much lacerated ; hut this is a slight evil, compared with the dread of the sharks and mantoravas (a monstrous kind of ray), which in every season make some their victims. For those reasons, it is difficult to prevail on a sufficient number of Indians to run the risk And, indeed, the trade is by no means so profitable as it was down to the end ol the last century. The net returns do not generally exceed twelve or fourteen thousand dollars in the six monihs þÿ viz., from May to October inclusive The pearls are usually sold by the owners of the boats in the gross, at so much per þÿpound (fifteen to
eighteen hundred piastres); þÿ and retailed by the purchasers at no little profit.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London, September 8, 1815. The French Policy in the China Seas. The Journal des Debuts publishes an article on the recent accounts received from China, which we subjoin at length. It is not a little remarkable to find it pointedly stated that the English are laying a tiap for the Chinese, in order to have an opportunity of seizing on some portion of the territories belonging to that empire which might answer the purposes of a commercial depot better than the island of Hong Ivong. The English are not in the habit of making use of such pretexts to gain their ends. The French, indeed, have been well known to lend themselves to transactions of the kind, as the Debuts well knows; for no one can forget thill it was under pretext of a debt due by Queen I'omaic that they seized upon the island of Tahiti. The fact, however, may possible turn out to be that France herself is about to seize upon au island in the Chinese seas, and the supposed intentions of England j ate put forward as au excuse for the violence

i i - a . which she is about to commit. The following is the article in question: þÿ (From the Journal des Debuts.) «' By the last East India tnai! we have received some interesting details with respect to the state of the English establishments in China. It appears that the island of Hong Kong, of which the sovereignty has been given to Great Britain, has not answered ihe expectations previously formed of it. It is a possession which seems condemned to perpetual insalubrity. It is a steril island, which does not produce in a year as much as will feed the inhabitants for eight davs It is good as the head quarters for the opium merchants, but it is now certain that it will never be a commercial place. It appears therefore that the English are already endeavouring to seeuie to themselves a better position. They have at present the island of Gluisan in their hands þÿ a position which is healthy and feitile, to which the great increase of the foreign commerce at Shang hai gives a great decree of importance, in a maritime, military, and conimetcial point of view. But they only hold Chusan as a guarantee, and the term of their occupation of it is limited to the 31st of December, 1845. It would, therefore, tie necessary for them to obtain from the Chinese government either a new runcession of the sovereignty of the island, or to find an oppoitunity of exact ing it. Some imprudent attacks on the part of the Chinese population, like that which took place at Macao on the person of Mr. Davis, the En-

glish commissioner, or that at Canton on Messrs. Montgomery, Martin, and Staunton, and for which the English have, perhaps designedly. deferred demanding reparation, mav probably in case of need, furnish the op/mi tumly which they are seeking. In the meantime they are expending a great deal of money at Chusan, and are lay ing tfie foundations of a durable establishment, " Some journals have asserted that French fotces having taken possession of the island of Basilan. the act had been disavowed by the government This assertion has been ofliciallv contradicted, and we are perfectly convinced that, even if there had bee.i entertained the wish to form a settlement in these seas so bad a choice as the island of Bastlan would never have been made. This island, moreover, has always been considered as a dependency tit Mandanao, which belongs to Spain. The Spanish monarchy has treaties with the Sultan of Soulon, sovereign of the islands of which Basilan is one. It lias also engagements with the chit f of these islands, who has conferred the protectorate of tfi in on Spain, and we have made too much account of the protectorate elsewhcie to fie capable of disputing its rights when vested in others. Many other considerations, also, must put away every thought of making an acquisition so ineligible as that of þÿBasilan. This small island, at the extremity of an archipelago carefully avoided by all nnvtgatots, and out of every course, could never ho converted to commerce. The utmost use to

which it could be turned would he as a military post, and this would be nugatory where there is no trade to protect. The archipelago of Soulon is the greatest nest of pirates in all the seas ot the world. England at one time obtained from a Sultan ol Soulon, the cease n of the island of Salemhangan, and the small garrison that was sent there was, in one night, very shortly aber its ariival, massacred to the last man. Spain has twice attempted

to establish herself in this terrible archipelago, and twice has she been driven out of it by the ferocious inhabitants. Basilan has ti verv fine harbour; but the country is mountainous, and covered with wood. During the south- <rn monsoon, whicli blows six months of the twelve, it is insupportably unhealthy. The produce of the islands is timber, Wax, motherof pearl, and a lish of which the Chinese are verj fond. But ail this together forms but a very miserable trade. This trade, which is represented as even more revolting than dealing in slaves, can only he carried on with arms in the. hand, because piracy is the onlv pursuit of the people of Basilan The little cultivation carried on in the islands is done by slaves brought from all quarters. In 1830, a fleet, composed of about 40 of their barks, manned by 2300 combatants, sailed round the large island of Lu$on, landed at every accessible point, and carried away an immense number of the Spumaids into slavery. At the same lime these bold pirates, so active at sea, so brave in fight, are, when at home, the most indolent of the human race. There, all the labour is done by the women and slaves; the warriors and seamen passing the whole of their time on shore in the most disgusting orgies. Tliey are so overcome bv their indigencies, that they remain till four or five o'clock in the day sleeping off the effects of the opium they have taken the night before. In this savage country, money is hardly known, and all the trade is carried

on bv barter. The great wealth is in the number of slaves. In short, from all the infoimaiion that has been gathered in a long series of years, we are led to believe that the opposition journals have put forth most gratuitous expressions of inquietude on the subject of this conquest, and that the occupation of the island of Basilan has never had anv existence other than in their own imaginations."

Queen Pomare, a docile and simple instrument of the Protestant missionaries, lias not accepted at our hands the portion of power which we offered. Far from it. In permanent rebellion against our establishment, this unfortunate woman places in our path every imaginable difficulty, the only way to remove which would be loestablish French sovereignty in the country. All competent judges who have returned from those distant countries are agreed in protesting against rendering the interior sovereignty to Queen Pomare, inasmuch as it is in reality giving it to th« missionaries. When France once decides upon planting her flag in nnv place she does not do it for the purpose of affording her enemies and those who envv tier the pleasuie of seeing her succumb to difficulties "

A short time before his death he addressed them as follows ; þÿ 'My children, he sure that God will reward you for what you have done for me; thanks to you. I am able to live in this house, from which 1 perceive that which was founded by the Abbe de I'Hj ee, who was once my ptotector. 1 shall soon die, and Imve very little to leave, but 1 entreat you not to sell the old arm chair in which I am seated, and which lias been with me these 50 veats It is an old friend, and I owe to it the preservation of my life on the 10th of August, 1702. I had then the honor of working for the King's upholsterer, and had just finished some hangings for the cabinet of Marie- Antoineite, when the Marseillais and the rebels of the Faubourg St. Autoine had their conflict with the Swiss. The palace being taken, 1 should have been massacred if my sense of danger had not inspired nie with the idea of tearing of) the skills of my coat and blackening my face with some soot from the chimney, so that 1 looked like one of the nssailunts When the pillage commenced I took up this arm chair, placed n on my head, and in this way traversed the hall'ol farts If yon have any

regard for me keep this old Royal arm-chair, and it will bring good luck to you ' A fortnight ago the old man died, and was decently interied by his nephews When they came to share the poor effects that he had left, they would have disputed as to who should have the old arm-chair if they had not both felt a respect for his injunctions.
